questions.question: Which of the following best defines an 'extra-axial' lesion?
choices: A lesion located within the brain parenchyma
A lesion located underneath the pial membrane
A lesion external to the pial membrane, involving meninges or CSF spaces
A lesion primarily involving the white matter tracts
A lesion originating from the ependymal lining
questions.detail: Intra-axial lesions are within the parenchyma underneath the pial membrane, whereas extra-axial lesions are external to the pial membrane, involving the meninges or CSF spaces.

questions.question: Which clinical triad is characteristic of Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH)?
choices: Hemiparesis, aphasia, and visual field defects
questions.detail: NPH is a form of communicating hydrocephalus defined by the specific clinical triad of ataxia, incontinence, and dementia.

questions.question: In cases of suspected NPH, which radiographic measurement is typically 'acute' or decreased?
questions.detail: The callosal angle is measured between the lateral ventricles on a coronal image; an acute or decreased angle is a characteristic imaging feature of NPH.

questions.question: The 'Kernohan notch phenomenon' leads to hemiparesis that is:
choices: Contralateral to the side of the herniation
Ipsilateral to the side of the herniation
questions.detail: Compression of the contralateral cerebral peduncle against the tentorial notch (the Kernohan notch) causes hemiparesis on the same side as the primary herniation.

questions.question: Small Duret hemorrhages within the medulla or brainstem are typically caused by:
choices: Shearing of perforating basilar artery branches due to downward force
Embolic spread from the Batson plexus
Venous hypertension from dural sinus thrombosis
questions.detail: Downward force on the brainstem during central herniation shears small perforating basilar artery branches, leading to Duret hemorrhages.

questions.question: 'Sunken skin flap syndrome' is a clinical manifestation of which condition?
questions.detail: Paradoxical herniation occurs after a large craniectomy when intracranial pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, causing the brain to shift away from the defect.

questions.question: Which of the following substances causes T1 shortening (hyperintensity on T1-weighted images)?
questions.detail: T1 shortening/hyperintensity is caused by several substances including fat, proteinaceous material, methemoglobin, and melanin.

questions.question: 'Flow-related enhancement' on T1-weighted spin-echo sequences refers to the hyperintense appearance of:
questions.detail: Flow-related enhancement is a time-of-flight effect where slow-flowing blood appears bright on T1-weighted images.

questions.question: Why do highly cellular tumors, such as lymphoma or medulloblastoma, typically appear hypointense on T2-weighted images?
questions.detail: A high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio in cellular tumors results in low lesional water content, which causes T2 shortening and hypointensity.

questions.question: On a T2-FLAIR sequence, how do white matter and gray matter signal intensities compare?
choices: White matter is brighter than gray matter
White matter is darker than gray matter
Gray matter is dark due to the inversion pulse
questions.detail: On T2-FLAIR images, white matter is darker than gray matter.

questions.question: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) primarily depicts which physical process?
questions.detail: DWI measures the random Brownian motion of water protons; reduced motion (as in acute ischemia) results in a bright signal.

questions.question: Which parameter determines the degree of diffusion weighting in a DWI sequence?
questions.detail: The b-value determines the degree of weighting based on the amplitude, duration, and timing of the diffusion gradients.

questions.question: In the setting of an acute infarct, diffusion is reduced within minutes due to:
choices: Failure of the Na/K ATPase pump leading to cytotoxic edema
questions.detail: Na/K ATPase pump failure leads to cytotoxic edema, shifting water from the extracellular to the restricted intracellular space.

questions.question: Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) is superior to standard GRE for distinguishing between:
questions.detail: SWI uses magnitude and phase images to help differentiate paramagnetic substances (like blood/iron) from diamagnetic substances (like calcification).

questions.question: In MR spectroscopy, 'Hunter’s angle' connects which three tall normal peaks?
questions.detail: Hunter’s angle refers to a line connecting the normal Choline, Creatine, and NAA peaks, which should point upward in a normal spectrum.

questions.question: Which metabolite peak, when present, indicates IDH-mutant status and a more favorable prognosis in gliomas?
questions.detail: 2-HG is a specific metabolic marker for IDH-mutant diffuse gliomas.

questions.question: Prominent lipid and lactate peaks on MRS are associated with which two conditions?
choices: High-grade gliomas (when nonenhancing) or lymphoma (when enhancing)
questions.detail: Lipid and lactate peaks suggest anaerobic metabolism or tissue damage, commonly seen in high-grade gliomas or lymphoma.

questions.question: According to the central volume equation used in MR perfusion, Cerebral Blood Flow (CBF) is equal to:
questions.detail: The central volume equation is defined as CBF = Cerebral Blood Volume (CBV) / Mean Transit Time (MTT).

questions.question: In the post-treatment setting for high-grade gliomas, an elevated Cerebral Blood Volume (CBV) favors:
questions.detail: Elevated CBV on perfusion imaging helps distinguish true tumor recurrence from treatment-related effects like radiation necrosis or pseudoprogression.

questions.question: Parenchymal enhancement following contrast administration is a direct marker of:
choices: Micro or macro disruption of the blood-brain barrier (BBB)
questions.detail: Enhancement in the brain parenchyma signifies that contrast has leaked out of the vasculature due to BBB disruption.

questions.question: Which CNS region normally enhances because it lacks a blood-brain barrier?
questions.detail: The area postrema, pituitary gland, and pineal gland are among several regions that normally enhance due to the lack of a BBB.

questions.question: Hematogenously disseminated metastatic disease is most commonly found at which location?
questions.detail: Metastatic emboli tend to lodge where the branching vasculature narrows at the subcortical gray-white junction.

questions.question: Smooth periventricular (subependymal) enhancement is characteristic of:
questions.detail: Linear, smooth enhancement along the ventricles is characteristic of ventriculitis or infectious ependymitis.

questions.question: The 'ivy sign' on FLAIR images is characteristic of which condition?
questions.detail: The ivy sign represents slow collateral flow within peripheral leptomeningeal vessels, a characteristic finding in moyamoya disease.

questions.question: Which finding distinguishes subarachnoid hemorrhage from leptomeningeal metastases on MRI?
choices: Blooming artifact on GRE or SWI
questions.detail: While both cause sulcal FLAIR hyperintensity, only subarachnoid hemorrhage will show blooming artifact on susceptibility-weighted sequences due to blood products.

questions.question: According to the 'MAGIC DR' mnemonic for ring-enhancing lesions, what does the 'D' represent?
questions.detail: MAGIC DR stands for Metastasis, Abscess, Glioma, Infarct, Contusion, Demyelination, and Radiation.

questions.question: What is the key finding that helps distinguish a demyelinating lesion from a tumor in cases of ring enhancement?
choices: Lack of significant mass effect relative to lesion size
Abnormal spectroscopy outside the lesion margin
questions.detail: Demyelinating lesions (such as MS) characteristically lack significant mass effect relative to their size and often show an incomplete 'C-shaped' ring of enhancement.

questions.question: Pachymeningeal enhancement on MRI refers to enhancement of which structure?
questions.detail: Pachymeninges refers specifically to the dura mater, while leptomeninges refers to the pia and arachnoid mater.

questions.question: Why is enhancement of the normal dura mater not typically visible on MRI?
choices: The blood-brain barrier is too tight
There is no blood flow to the dura
There are normally very few water protons in the dura
Gadolinium does not enter the dural space
questions.detail: MRI enhancement requires both contrast and water protons; the normal dura contains few water protons, so visible enhancement usually indicates dural edema.

questions.question: Smooth, linear dural enhancement and 'sagging' of the cerebellar tonsils are features of:
questions.detail: Intracranial hypotension leads to prolonged low CSF pressure, resulting in reactive dural enhancement and downward displacement (sagging) of brain structures.

questions.question: A 'dural tail' is a focal area of reactive dural enhancement most commonly associated with:
questions.detail: A dural tail is a classic imaging finding associated with meningiomas.

questions.question: Which condition presents with gyriform enhancement and restricted diffusivity, typically starting in the medial temporal lobes?
questions.detail: HSV encephalitis is a necrotizing infection characteristically showing gyral enhancement and restricted diffusion in the temporal lobes and limbic system.

questions.question: SMART syndrome (stroke-like migraine attacks after radiation therapy) is a delayed complication occurring:
choices: During the first week of treatment
questions.detail: SMART syndrome is a late complication of radiotherapy, often occurring years or decades after the initial treatment.

questions.question: Gyriform enhancement in a subacute infarct typically lasts for which duration?
choices: Only until the mass effect peaks
questions.detail: In a late subacute infarct, gyriform enhancement typically begins around 6 days and can last up to 6 weeks.

questions.question: Which drug or therapy is known to artifactually increase subarachnoid FLAIR signal in the absence of hemorrhage or meningitis?
questions.detail: Administration of high-flow oxygen or propofol can cause artifactually bright signal in the subarachnoid space on FLAIR images, mimicking hemorrhage.
